subChunks.title: CSS Layers and Cascade Management
subChunks.hookHtml: CSS specificity wars are the root cause of most !important abuse. CSS @layer gives you explicit control over the cascade order — Tailwind v4 uses layers internally, and understanding them lets you integrate third-party CSS, base styles, and custom utilities without specificity conflicts.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Maester Cordell: "Every !important in a codebase is a confession that someone lost a specificity battle they did not understand. @layer removes the battle entirely. You declare the order; the cascade respects it."

How @layer works

Layers have explicit precedence order. A rule in a higher-priority layer beats a rule in a lower-priority layer regardless of specificity:

/* Declare layer order — last listed wins in conflicts */
@layer base, components, utilities;

@layer base {
  /* Low priority — can be overridden by components or utilities */
  h1 { font-size: 2rem; }
  p  { line-height: 1.6; }
}

@layer components {
  .card { background: white; border-radius: 0.5rem; padding: 1rem; }
}

@layer utilities {
  /* Highest priority — wins over base and components */
  .text-red-500 { color: rgb(239 68 68); }
}

/* Unlayered CSS is treated as above all layers */
.override { font-size: 1rem !important; }  /* Only use as last resort */

Tailwind v4's layer structure

/* When you @import "tailwindcss", Tailwind emits: */
@layer theme { /* CSS variables from @theme */ }
@layer base { /* normalize, default element styles */ }
@layer components { /* @utility definitions */ }
@layer utilities { /* generated utility classes */ }

/* Your custom CSS can extend or override these layers: */
@layer base {
  /* Add to Tailwind's base layer */
  *, *::before, *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  :focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid var(--color-primary);
    outline-offset: 2px;
  }
}

@layer components {
  /* Component styles that Tailwind utilities can still override */
  .prose-custom {
    max-width: 65ch;
    line-height: 1.75;
  }
}

Integrating third-party CSS without specificity conflicts

/* Wrap third-party CSS in a low-priority layer */
@layer vendor {
  @import "third-party-library.css";
}

/* Declare vendor below your layers so it never wins */
@layer vendor, base, components, utilities;

The specificity chart with @layer

/* Specificity order (lowest to highest): */
/* 1. @layer vendor                         */
/* 2. @layer base                           */
/* 3. @layer components                     */
/* 4. @layer utilities                      */
/* 5. Unlayered CSS                         */
/* 6. !important (within layers, reversed)  */

/* A class in utilities ALWAYS beats a class in base, */
/* even if the base rule has higher selector specificity. */

When to use @layer components vs @utility

/* @utility — for single-responsibility utilities */
@utility scrollbar-hide { scrollbar-width: none; }
@utility focus-ring { outline: 2px solid var(--color-primary); }

/* @layer components — for multi-property component patterns */
@layer components {
  .input-base {
    width: 100%;
    padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
    border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
    border-radius: 0.375rem;
    font-size: 0.875rem;
    transition: border-color 0.15s;
  }
}
/* Tailwind utilities can still override: */
<input class="input-base border-red-500"> /* Overrides border-color from @layer components */

Maester Cordell: "The rule: @utility for single-purpose reusable utilities. @layer components for multi-property base styles that utilities will override. @layer vendor for third-party CSS. Never reach for !important when @layer solves it."

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: @layer gives you explicit cascade order. A utility class in @layer utilities always beats a component style in @layer components — regardless of selector specificity. This is how Tailwind wins every style conflict without !important.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a form input system using @layer components for base styles that Tailwind utilities override:

  • .layer-input: w-full, px-3, py-2, border, border-gray-300, rounded-md, text-sm, focus:outline-none, focus-visible:ring-2, focus-visible:ring-blue-500, focus-visible:border-blue-500, transition-colors
  • .layer-input-error: w-full, px-3, py-2, border, border-red-500, rounded-md, text-sm, focus:outline-none, focus-visible:ring-2, focus-visible:ring-red-500, transition-colors
  • .layer-label: block, text-sm, font-medium, text-gray-700, mb-1
  • .layer-hint: text-xs, text-gray-500, mt-1
  • .layer-error-msg: text-xs, text-red-600, mt-1

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a demonstration of @layer cascade management from scratch. Create three CSS rules — one in @layer base, one in @layer components, one in @layer utilities — that all set the same property on the same selector. Show that the utilities layer wins. Write a comment explaining why, even if the base rule has a higher specificity selector.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why @layer makes !important largely unnecessary in a Tailwind codebase. Walk through how Tailwind v4 uses layers internally, and explain the correct use case for @utility vs @layer components for a new reusable class.

questions.prompt: Given @layer base, components, utilities declared in this order, a rule in @layer utilities with specificity (0,1,0) and a rule in @layer base with specificity (1,0,0) — which wins?
options: The @layer utilities rule wins — layer order overrides selector specificity
The @layer base rule wins — specificity (1,0,0) is higher
Both apply — they are in different layers so no conflict occurs
The one declared later in the source file wins
questions.answer: The @layer utilities rule wins — layer order overrides selector specificity
questions.explanation: @layer explicitly overrides specificity within the cascade. The layer declared later in the @layer order always wins, regardless of selector specificity. This is the entire point: utilities always override base styles without needing higher specificity selectors or !important.

questions.prompt: You are integrating a third-party CSS library that sets font-size on .card. Tailwind's text-sm should override it but doesn't. What is the most elegant fix using @layer?
options: Wrap the library import in @layer vendor { ... } and declare: @layer vendor, base, components, utilities — utilities always win
Add !important to the text-sm Tailwind utility
Load the third-party CSS after Tailwind so it takes precedence by source order
questions.answer: Wrap the library import in @layer vendor { ... } and declare: @layer vendor, base, components, utilities — utilities always win
questions.explanation: Wrapping third-party CSS in a low-priority @layer vendor places it below all Tailwind layers in the cascade. Any Tailwind utility then wins the conflict without !important or increased specificity. Loading third-party CSS last in source order would make it win, not Tailwind.

questions.prompt: You want to create a reusable .input-base class with multiple properties (padding, border, font-size) that Tailwind utilities can still override. Should you use @utility or @layer components?
options: @layer components — multi-property component styles that Tailwind's utilities layer overrides
@utility — all custom CSS should be defined as @utility to participate in Tailwind's system
Either works identically — the choice is purely stylistic
@utility for multi-property styles; @layer components for single-property utilities
questions.answer: @layer components — multi-property component styles that Tailwind's utilities layer overrides
questions.explanation: @utility is for single-responsibility utilities (like .scrollbar-hide) that should behave like Tailwind built-ins — participating in the utilities layer. @layer components is for multi-property component base styles that are meant to be extended by utility classes. Tailwind utilities in @layer utilities always override @layer components, so the override pattern works correctly.
